title: Bookcases as Gardens
hookLine: a small Jewish library: Tanakh, siddur, a Haggadah, a book of stories
carry: holy books are companions, never thrown away
tomorrow: a nicer cup for the same blessing. does that matter to God?

lines: ONE HEAVY BOX AT A TIME.
A FATHER'S LETTER TO HIS SON.
cards: Moving house tells you exactly how many books you own, one heavy box at a time, and someone always asks whether you really need them all.

A father named Judah ibn Tibbon, a translator, left his son a long letter about how to live, and he spent part of it on books. Make your books your companions, he wrote, and let your bookcases be your gardens.

teach.b: He keeps going: pick their fruit, gather their flowers, walk through them. A shelf isn't storage; it's somewhere you stroll. A Jewish home doesn't need a big library to start that garden.
Here's one small shelf: a Tanakh, the Hebrew Bible; a siddur, the prayer book; a Haggadah for the Passover seder; and a book of stories, for the nights when the big books feel too big.

In this tradition, books are treated almost like people. The Shulchan Aruch, a code of Jewish law, says not to sit on a bench where a holy book is lying, and not to use one as a stand for something else.
Some people kiss a holy book if it falls, as you'd help up a friend. And when a holy book wears out, it isn't thrown away.
It's buried, or set aside in a geniza, a storeroom for worn sacred pages, until it can be.

So the question for a crowded move isn't only how many books, but which ones you'd walk among. Something to tell a friend tonight: a father once left his son a letter telling him to treat his bookshelves like a garden.

how: Jewish homes may keep a Tanakh, a siddur and a Haggadah on the shelf; holy books are handled with care, and worn-out ones are placed in a synagogue's geniza or buried rather than thrown away.

games.q: your kid's prayer book is falling apart, pages loose and torn. what does the tradition do with it?
o: set it aside for a geniza, or bury it.
put it in the recycling with the newspapers.
tape it shut and keep it in a drawer, unused.
games.why: worn-out holy books aren't thrown away; they're buried, or rest in a geniza until they can be.

practice: Pick up one book near you, a Jewish one if you have it. Hold it like a guest: notice the cover, the weight, the page it falls open to.
Then decide where it would live best, at eye level, near where you sit, easy to reach for its fruit.

wordCard.voice: Books at home: a small garden of them, Tanakh, siddur, Haggadah, stories, treated with honor and never just thrown out.

orig.note: Hebrew: books; one book is a sefer.

carryVoice: Something to keep: holy books are companions, never thrown away. Walk among them like a garden. Thirteen of fifteen, shelved.

sources.ref: Judah ibn Tibbon, ethical will to his son (make your books your companions; your bookcases your gardens)
Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 282 (honoring holy books: not sitting on a bench where one lies; not using one for another purpose)
Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 26b (worn holy objects and books are stored away or buried)
